visual.caption: Thirteen ideas, one purpose: accounts that can be compared and trusted.

slides.narration: Welcome to Class eleven accountancy. Every shop, factory and school keeps accounts in much the same way, and this is no accident. Accountants follow shared rules called generally accepted accounting principles. In this part we study thirteen basic ideas, the concepts and conventions, and apply them to imagined businesses: valuing land, matching expenses to revenue, and valuing stock with caution.

slides.heading: GAAP: the common rulebook
slides.body_md: **GAAP** are the rules, concepts and conventions that accountants follow to make accounts uniform.

rows: The rules, concepts and conventions followed in recording transactions and preparing statements
Uniform accounts that can be compared and relied on

visual.alt: Table of GAAP: full form, what they are, their purpose, and their two parts, concepts and conventions

slides.narration: Generally accepted accounting principles are the rules, concepts and conventions that accountants follow when they record transactions and prepare statements. Their purpose is uniformity. When two firms follow the same principles, their accounts can be compared and trusted by owners, lenders and tax officers. Concepts are the basic assumptions of accounting, and conventions are the accepted customs that guide how the statements are prepared.

slides.heading: The firm, its money and its life

rows: The business is a unit separate from its owner
A household bill paid from the till is the owner's drawings
Only events expressible in money are recorded
An oven bought for ₹85,000 is recorded; a baker's skill is not
The firm is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future
A machine is written off over its life, not valued at a forced-sale price

visual.alt: Table of three concepts: business entity, money measurement and going concern, each with its meaning and an imagined case

slides.narration: Three concepts describe the firm itself. The business entity concept treats the business as separate from its owner, so a household bill paid from the till is the owner's drawings. Money measurement records only what can be expressed in money, so an oven is recorded but a baker's skill is not. The going concern concept assumes the firm will continue, so a machine is written off over its life.

slides.heading: Quick check: whose payment is it?
slides.body_md: A shop owner pays a family bill from the shop's cash box.
slides.narration: Read the situation carefully. Ask yourself who benefits from the payment, the shop or its owner, and how the business entity concept treats a payment that benefits the owner personally.

slides.heading: Period, price and proof

rows: Profit and position are found at regular intervals, usually twelve months
Assets are recorded at the price actually paid
Land bought for ₹10,00,000 stays at that figure
A purchase is recorded on the supplier's invoice

visual.alt: Table of accounting period, cost and objectivity with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: The accounting period concept says profit and position are found at regular intervals, usually twelve months, such as the first of April to the thirty first of March. The cost concept records an asset at the price actually paid. Objectivity asks that every entry rest on verifiable evidence, such as the supplier's invoice, so that two accountants would reach the same figure.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cost against market value
slides.body_md: **Kaveri Printers**, an imagined firm, bought land for ₹18,00,000. Similar land now sells for ₹27,00,000.
bullets: The balance sheet shows **₹18,00,000**: the price paid.
The rise of ₹9,00,000 is not recorded until the land is sold.
Cost is objective and verifiable; a market value is an opinion that keeps changing.

rows: Cost of the land (recorded in the balance sheet)
Rise as a per cent of cost

visual.alt: Table for Kaveri Printers: land recorded at cost 18,00,000 rupees, market value 27,00,000 rupees, unrecorded rise 9,00,000 rupees, which is 50 per cent of cost

slides.narration: Kaveri Printers bought land for rupees eighteen lakh. Similar land now sells for rupees twenty seven lakh. Under the cost concept the balance sheet still shows rupees eighteen lakh. The rise of rupees nine lakh, which is half of the cost, is not recorded, because the land has not been sold and a market value is only an opinion. The price paid can be proved from the deed and the payment.

slides.heading: Dual aspect: the basis of the equation
slides.body_md: Every transaction has **two aspects** of equal value, so Assets = Liabilities + Capital after every transaction.

visual.alt: Flow: every transaction affects two items by equal values, so assets always equal liabilities plus capital
visual.caption: Two sides, always equal.

slides.narration: The dual aspect concept says that every transaction has two sides of equal value. When a firm buys furniture for cash, one asset rises and another falls by the same amount. When it buys goods on credit, an asset and a liability rise together. Because of this, assets always equal liabilities plus capital, and this accounting equation is the basis of double entry book-keeping.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the equation step by step
slides.body_md: The imagined **Tara Stationers** starts with cash as capital. After each step, assets equal liabilities plus capital.
bullets: Buying furniture changes one asset for another.
Credit purchase and loan raise an asset and a liability together.
Owner's personal use of cash reduces cash and capital.

rows: Owner took cash ₹5,000 for personal use

visual.alt: Accounting equation table for Tara Stationers: after six steps cash is 1,15,000, furniture 40,000, stock 30,000, creditors 20,000, bank loan 20,000 and capital 1,45,000 rupees; assets of 1,85,000 equal liabilities plus capital

slides.narration: Tara Stationers starts with rupees one lakh fifty thousand in cash as capital. Buying furniture only swaps cash for furniture. Goods on credit and a bank loan raise an asset and a liability together. Paying a creditor lowers cash and creditors. When the owner takes cash for personal use, cash and capital fall. At the end, assets of rupees one lakh eighty five thousand equal outside liabilities plus capital of rupees one lakh forty five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: going concern
slides.body_md: A firm has decided to close at the end of the month.
slides.narration: Think about what the going concern concept assumes. If a firm has already decided to close down, is that assumption still true, and what should the machinery be valued at?

slides.heading: Revenue recognition and matching

rows: Revenue is recognised when it is earned, that is when the sale is made, not when cash is received
A sofa delivered in December and paid for in January is December revenue
The expenses of a period are set against the revenue of the same period
Insurance for twelve months is charged only for the months used in the year

visual.alt: Table of revenue recognition and matching with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Revenue recognition says revenue belongs to the period in which it is earned, that is when the sale is made, whether or not cash has come in. The matching concept then sets the expenses of the period against that revenue. Insurance paid for twelve months is charged only for the months used in the year, and the rest is carried forward as a prepaid expense.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: profit of a month by matching
slides.body_md: **Anjali Tailors**, an imagined shop, October 2026. Sales on cash and credit are revenue; expenses are those of October only.
bullets: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock = ₹70,000.
Rent paid of ₹16,000 covers two months, so ₹8,000 is charged and ₹8,000 carried forward.

rows: Revenue earned: sales of the month
Less: rent of October only (16,000 paid for 2 months)

visual.alt: Matching table for Anjali Tailors, October 2026: sales 1,20,000, cost of goods sold 70,000, salaries 15,000, rent 8,000, electricity 2,000, profit 25,000 rupees

slides.narration: Anjali Tailors earned sales of rupees one lakh twenty thousand in October. The cost of goods sold is opening stock plus purchases less closing stock, which is rupees seventy thousand. Salaries of the month are rupees fifteen thousand, including the part still due. Rent paid covers two months, so only rupees eight thousand is charged. With electricity, the profit of the month is rupees twenty five thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit by matching
slides.body_md: Find the profit by charging only the expenses that belong to the month.
slides.narration: Work in three steps. First find the cost of goods sold, then the salary and rent that belong to the month alone, and finally subtract all the expenses from the sales.

slides.heading: Full disclosure and consistency

rows: All facts that could influence users are shown in the statements or in notes
A pending court claim is reported in a note
The same methods are followed from period to period
Depreciation is charged by one method year after year

visual.alt: Table of full disclosure and consistency with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Full disclosure asks that every fact that could influence the decisions of users be shown, in the statements or in notes, such as a pending court claim. Consistency asks that the same accounting methods be followed from period to period, so that the results of different years can be compared. A method may be changed for a good reason, but the change and its effect must be disclosed.

slides.heading: Conservatism and materiality

rows: Provide for all possible losses; do not anticipate profits
Stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value
Items large enough to influence decisions are shown separately; trivial items are treated simply
A sharpener costing a few rupees is expensed at once

visual.alt: Table of conservatism and materiality with meanings and imagined cases

slides.narration: Conservatism, also called prudence, asks the accountant to provide for all possible losses but not to anticipate any profit. That is why closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Materiality says that only items large enough to influence decisions need separate treatment, so a very small item such as a sharpener may be treated as an expense at once.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value
slides.body_md: **Sagar Electricals**, an imagined shop, values each item of closing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
bullets: Fans and air coolers stay at cost: the expected gain is not recorded.
Heaters and irons are written down to net realisable value: the loss of ₹14,000 is provided for.

visual.alt: Table for Sagar Electricals: stock of 1,40,000 rupees at cost and 1,37,000 rupees at net realisable value is valued item by item at 1,26,000 rupees, a write-down of 14,000 rupees

slides.narration: Sagar Electricals compares cost with net realisable value for each item. Fans and air coolers could fetch more than they cost, but the gain is not recorded, so they stay at cost. Heaters and irons would fetch less, so they are written down. Stock at cost is rupees one lakh forty thousand, and the value taken is rupees one lakh twenty six thousand, a write down of rupees fourteen thousand.

slides.heading: Quick check: valuing stock
slides.body_md: Fill in the blanks about closing stock and caution.
slides.narration: Recall the rule for valuing closing stock. It compares two values and takes the lower one. Which two values, and which concept explains why we take the lower?

slides.heading: Which concept applies?

rows: The owner pays a household bill from the till
Insurance paid for twelve months is charged for the months used
Stock is valued below cost because its selling price fell
The same depreciation method is used every year
A very small item is expensed at once
A purchase is entered only after the invoice arrives

visual.alt: Table matching six situations to the concepts they illustrate

slides.narration: Here are six situations and the concept behind each. A household bill from the till is business entity. Insurance charged only for months used is matching. Stock valued below cost is conservatism. The same depreciation method every year is consistency. A tiny item expensed at once is materiality. A purchase entered only after the invoice is objectivity.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: **GAAP** make accounts uniform and comparable.
Concepts: business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost, dual aspect, revenue recognition, matching, objectivity.
Conventions: full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality.

rows: Business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period, cost
Full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality, objectivity

visual.alt: Summary table grouping the thirteen concepts and conventions into what is recorded, how it is recorded and how it is reported

slides.narration: To sum up. Generally accepted accounting principles make accounts uniform and comparable. Some concepts say what is recorded, such as the entity, money, the going concern, the period and cost. Others say how it is recorded, through dual aspect, revenue recognition and matching. The conventions of full disclosure, consistency, conservatism and materiality guide how the results are reported.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define the concept in one line, then give a small imagined example.
In stock questions, compare cost and net realisable value for every item.
Remember: matching charges only the months used; the rest is carried forward.

rows: Name the concept and say why it applies
Marks go to the reasoning, not only the label
Show the working for stock and matching
Method marks are given even if the final figure slips
Give a small example for each concept
It proves you understand the idea

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the concepts and conventions

slides.narration: In the examination, define each concept in one line and add a small example. For stock questions, compare cost with net realisable value for every item, and show your working. In matching questions, charge only the months that belong to the period and carry the rest forward as prepaid. Always name the concept in your answer.

slides.narration: In this part we ask three questions. When should a transaction be recorded, when the cash moves or when the revenue is earned? Why do accountants follow written standards, and who issues them in India? And how does goods and services tax work, with its central, state and integrated parts and its input tax credit? All figures belong to imagined businesses.

slides.heading: Two bases of accounting

visual.alt: Table of the cash basis and the accrual basis: when revenue and expenses are recorded

slides.narration: There are two bases of accounting. On the cash basis, revenue is recorded when cash is received and an expense when cash is paid. On the accrual basis, revenue is recorded when it is earned and an expense when it is incurred, whether or not cash has moved. Most businesses use the accrual basis, because it matches expenses to revenue.

slides.heading: The same event, two treatments

rows: Fees for November received in October
Rent for March paid in April
Goods sold on credit in June, cash received in July

visual.alt: Table showing in which period three events are recorded under the cash basis and under the accrual basis

slides.narration: Look at three events. Fees for November received in October count as October revenue on the cash basis, but November revenue on the accrual basis. Rent for March paid in April is an April expense on the cash basis, but a March expense on the accrual basis. A credit sale in June paid for in July is June revenue on the accrual basis.

slides.heading: Quick check: rent paid late
slides.body_md: Rent for one month is paid in the next month.
slides.narration: The cash basis follows the movement of cash. Think about the month in which the rent is actually paid, and compare it with the month to which the rent belongs.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: profit under both bases
slides.body_md: **Meghna Coaching Classes**, an imagined tuition centre, October 2026.
bullets: Cash received ₹90,000, of which ₹20,000 is advance for November and ₹15,000 is arrears of September.
Fees of ₹12,000 earned in October are still due.
Rent ₹24,000 was paid for 3 months; salary paid ₹30,000 includes ₹6,000 of September, and ₹7,000 is due.

slides.heading: Accounting standards: meaning and need

rows: Written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for treating and disclosing items
Statements of different firms and years can be compared
Rules limit personal judgement, so figures can be trusted
A narrower choice of methods reduces manipulation

visual.alt: Table on accounting standards: their meaning and the needs of comparability, reliability and fewer alternatives

slides.narration: Accounting standards are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for treating and disclosing items in financial statements. They are needed for three reasons. They make statements comparable across firms and years. They make figures more reliable by limiting personal judgement. And they reduce the number of alternative methods, so there is less room to present figures in a favourable way.

It is destination based, so the tax goes to the place of consumption. It has a dual structure, and it allows input tax credit, so that tax falls only on the value added at each stage.

**GAAP** (generally accepted accounting principles) are the rules, concepts and conventions that accountants follow in recording transactions and preparing financial statements. Their purpose is **uniformity**: statements of different firms and different years can be compared and relied on.

**Concepts** are the basic assumptions on which accounting rests. **Conventions** are customs and guidelines that have become accepted. The diagram groups thirteen ideas into what is recorded, how it is recorded and how it is reported.

sections.heading: 2. The firm, its money and its time
sections.body_md:
**Business entity:** the business is a unit separate from its owner; the owner's personal payments are **drawings**.

**Money measurement:** only events that can be expressed in money are recorded.

**Going concern:** the firm is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future, so assets are written off over their lives, not valued at forced-sale prices.

**Accounting period:** profit and position are found at regular intervals, usually twelve months.

**Cost (historical cost):** an asset is recorded at the price actually paid; later market changes are not recorded. **Objectivity:** entries rest on verifiable evidence such as bills and vouchers.

sections.heading: 3. Dual aspect, revenue recognition and matching
sections.body_md:
**Dual aspect:** every transaction has two aspects of equal value; hence **Assets = Liabilities + Capital** holds after every transaction. It is the basis of double entry.

**Revenue recognition (realisation):** revenue is recognised when it is earned, that is when the sale is made, not when cash is received. Advance received is a liability until the goods are delivered.

**Matching:** the expenses of a period are set against the revenue of the same period. Outstanding expenses are added; prepaid expenses are carried forward.

sections.body_md:
**Full disclosure:** all facts that could influence users are shown in the statements or notes.

**Consistency:** the same methods are followed from period to period; a change needs a reason and disclosure.

**Conservatism (prudence):** provide for all possible losses; do not anticipate profits. Closing stock is valued at the **lower of cost and net realisable value**.

**Materiality:** items large enough to influence decisions are shown separately; trivial items may be treated simply.

sections.heading: 5. Bases of accounting and accounting standards
sections.body_md:
**Cash basis:** revenue is recorded when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. **Accrual basis:** revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred; advances, arrears, prepaid and outstanding items are adjusted.

**Accounting standards** are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies. **Need:** comparability, reliability, fewer alternative methods. **Benefits:** uniform practice, trusted figures, easier audit, fair comparison.

**Dated note (as of 2024):** in India standards are issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India through its Accounting Standards Board (set up in 1977). **Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)** are converged with International Financial Reporting Standards; notified by the government in 2015 and applicable from the 2016 financial year to specified companies.

sections.heading: 6. Goods and services tax (GST)
sections.body_md:
**As of 2024.** GST is an **indirect tax** on the supply of goods and services, **destination-based** (the tax accrues to the place of consumption), introduced on **1 July 2017**.

**Dual structure:** on an intra-state supply, **CGST** (Centre) and **SGST** (state; **UTGST** in Union Territories) in equal parts; on an inter-state supply, **IGST**, collected by the Centre and shared with the destination state.

**Input tax credit:** tax paid on purchases is set off against tax payable on sales; tax falls only on value added. **GSTIN:** the 15-character identification number of a registered taxpayer. Rates are not fixed in these notes; every problem states an imagined rate.

questions.stem_md: A newly appointed accountant at an imagined trading firm asks why every firm should follow generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). The best answer is that GAAP

options.text_md: fix the profit that each firm must earn in a year
make the accounts of different firms uniform, so that they can be compared and relied on
tell a firm which goods it is allowed to sell
remove the need to keep books of account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** make the accounts of different firms uniform, so that they can be compared and relied on. GAAP are the accepted rules, concepts and conventions of accounting; their purpose is uniformity and comparability. They do not fix profits, control what a firm sells, or replace the books of account.

questions.stem_md: Meera Sharma owns Meera Handlooms, an imagined shop in Ranipur. On 4 June 2026 she paid her daughter's tuition fee of ₹9,000 from the shop's cash box. By the business entity concept, this payment is

options.text_md: recorded as tuition expense of the shop
recorded as an asset of the shop
left out because it is small
treated as drawings, not as an expense of the shop

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** treated as drawings, not as an expense of the shop. The business is a separate unit from its owner, so a personal payment is the owner's drawings; it reduces capital and cash. It is not a business expense or asset, and size is irrelevant to the entity concept.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following can be recorded in the books of Orchid Bakers, an imagined bakery, under the money measurement concept?

options.text_md: Purchase of an oven for ₹85,000
The excellent skill of the head baker
The loyalty of regular customers
The friendly relations between the owner and the staff

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Purchase of an oven for ₹85,000. Only events that can be expressed in money are recorded. The purchase has a price; skill, loyalty and goodwill of relations have no money value in the books until they are measured by a transaction.

questions.stem_md: A hardware firm owns a machine that cost ₹5,00,000 and will serve for ten more years. The firm shows it at cost less depreciation, and not at the price it would fetch in a forced sale next week. This follows the

options.text_md: conservatism concept
materiality concept
going concern concept
revenue recognition concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** going concern concept. A firm is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future, so its assets are used up over their life and written off through depreciation; a forced-sale price is relevant only if closure is expected. Conservatism concerns caution about profit, materiality concerns importance of items, and revenue recognition concerns the timing of income.

questions.stem_md: Why does an imagined firm prepare its accounts for a fixed period, usually twelve months, instead of waiting until the business is closed?

options.text_md: Because the law fixes the profit for each year
Because assets lose value only once a year
To measure profit and financial position at regular intervals, since the business is expected to continue
Because transactions cannot be recorded in a shorter time

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To measure profit and financial position at regular intervals, since the business is expected to continue. A continuing business needs periodic results for owners, lenders and tax. The law does not fix profits, assets can lose value at any time, and transactions are recorded as they occur.

questions.stem_md: Kaveri Printers, an imagined firm, bought land for ₹18,00,000 in 2021. Similar land in the area now sells for ₹27,00,000. Under the cost concept, the balance sheet shows the land at
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹18,00,000. The asset stays at the price actually paid, ₹18,00,000. ₹27,00,000 is the current market value, which is not recorded; ₹9,00,000 is only the unrecorded rise; and ₹45,00,000 adds the two values without meaning.

questions.stem_md: Sunil Fabrics, an imagined firm, buys a sewing machine on credit from a supplier. By the dual aspect concept, the effect on the accounting equation is

options.text_md: an increase in an asset and a decrease in capital
a decrease in a liability and an increase in capital
an increase in one asset with no other change
an increase in an asset and an equal increase in a liability

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an increase in an asset and an equal increase in a liability. The machine (asset) increases and the amount owed to the supplier (liability) increases by the same value, so Assets = Liabilities + Capital still holds. Capital does not change on a credit purchase, and no transaction affects only one item.

questions.stem_md: Anil Furnishers, an imagined firm, delivered a sofa set priced at ₹30,000 to a customer on 28 December 2026 on credit. The customer paid on 10 January 2027. By the revenue recognition concept, the revenue is recognised in

options.text_md: January 2027, when the cash was received
December 2026, when the goods were delivered and the sale was made
the month in which the customer first enquired about the sofa set
both months, half in each

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** December 2026, when the goods were delivered and the sale was made. Revenue is recognised when it is earned, that is when the goods pass to the buyer and the right to receive the price arises, not when cash comes in. An enquiry earns nothing, and revenue is not split over two months.

questions.stem_md: Pooja Dairy, an imagined business, pays the December salaries of its staff on 5 January. The salaries are charged against the revenue of December and shown as a liability on 31 December. This applies the

options.text_md: matching concept
cost concept
money measurement concept
business entity concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** matching concept. Expenses are set against the revenue they helped to earn in the same period, whatever the date of payment. The cost, money measurement and entity concepts do not decide in which period an expense falls.

questions.stem_md: Lotus Chemicals, an imagined company, faces a court claim of ₹4,00,000 that may turn into a liability next year. The accountant mentions it in a note to the balance sheet. This follows the

options.text_md: materiality concept
full disclosure concept
objectivity concept
cost concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** full disclosure concept. Full disclosure requires that all information that could influence the decisions of users be shown. A note on a possible liability serves that purpose. Materiality is about leaving out trivial items, objectivity about verifiable evidence, and cost about the recording price of assets.

questions.stem_md: Rohan Traders, an imagined firm, charged depreciation by the straight line method in 2025-26. It plans to switch to the written down value method in 2026-27 only to show a lower profit for that year. The plan goes against the

options.text_md: going concern concept
business entity concept
consistency concept
money measurement concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** consistency concept. Consistency requires the same accounting methods from period to period so that results can be compared; a change is acceptable only for a good reason and with disclosure. Switching merely to alter profit breaks it. The other concepts are not concerned with method.

questions.stem_md: At the year end, Neha Bookstore, an imagined shop, finds that books costing ₹60,000 can now be sold only for ₹52,000. Following the conservatism concept, these books appear in closing stock at
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹52,000. Stock is valued at the lower of cost, ₹60,000, and net realisable value, ₹52,000, so that an expected loss is provided for. ₹60,000 ignores the fall, ₹8,000 is only the fall, and ₹1,12,000 adds two values.

questions.stem_md: Which treatment shows the materiality concept at work in Girnar Steel Works, an imagined large factory?

options.text_md: A new furnace costing ₹90,00,000 is charged to expense in the year of purchase
A court claim of ₹50,00,000 against the factory is left out of the accounts
Sales of ₹2,00,00,000 are shown as ₹1,50,00,000
A stapler costing ₹120 is charged to expense in the year of purchase although it lasts several years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A stapler costing ₹120 is charged to expense in the year of purchase although it lasts several years. Materiality allows an insignificant item to be treated in the simplest way, since showing it as an asset would not change any decision. The furnace, the claim and the sales figure are all large enough to matter, and the other treatments distort the accounts.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of Ujwal Opticals, an imagined firm, records a purchase of ₹36,000 only after receiving the supplier's invoice. This practice reflects the

options.text_md: going concern concept
matching concept
objectivity concept
conservatism concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** objectivity concept. Objectivity means that entries are supported by verifiable evidence such as an invoice, so that anyone checking would reach the same figure. Going concern, matching and conservatism deal with continuity, periods and caution.

questions.stem_md: Sagar Electricals, an imagined shop, holds one lot of mixers that cost ₹30,000. A new model has lowered their expected selling price, so that their net realisable value is ₹24,000. At what amount should the lot appear in closing stock?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹24,000. The lower of ₹30,000 and ₹24,000 is ₹24,000. ₹30,000 would carry the expected loss into the next year; ₹6,000 is the write-down, not the value; and ₹54,000 adds the two figures.

questions.stem_md: Tanvi Textiles, an imagined firm, paid ₹36,000 on 1 October 2026 as insurance premium for the twelve months beginning that day, and charged the whole amount as an expense of the year ended 31 March 2027. Which statement about this treatment is correct?

options.text_md: The expense of the year is overstated by ₹18,000, because only six months of cover were used in the year
The treatment is correct because the cash was paid in that year
The expense of the year is understated by ₹18,000
The treatment is correct under the cost concept

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The expense of the year is overstated by ₹18,000, because only six months of cover were used in the year. Six of the twelve months fall in the year, so the charge is ₹18,000; the remaining ₹18,000 belongs to the next year and is carried forward as a prepaid expense (matching concept). The year's expense is therefore overstated, not understated, and the date of payment does not decide the period. The cost concept does not apply to expenses of a period.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The accounting equation remains balanced after every transaction.

**Reason (R):** Every transaction has a two-sided effect of equal value on the accounts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true. Because each transaction changes two items by equal amounts, the two sides of Assets = Liabilities + Capital stay equal, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sagar Electricals values its closing stock at the lower of cost and net realisable value.

**Reason (R):** Fixed assets are recorded at the price paid to acquire them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true: stock valuation follows conservatism and fixed assets follow the cost concept. But the cost of acquiring fixed assets says nothing about why stock is written down to a lower realisable value, so R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the going concern concept, accounts may be prepared only at the end of the life of the business.

**Reason (R):** Under the going concern concept, a business is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the concept supports periodic accounts for a business expected to continue; accounts are not limited to the end of its life. R is true and states the concept correctly.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the materiality concept, a trivial item may be treated in the simplest way.

**Reason (R):** Under the materiality concept, every item, however small, must be shown separately in the financial statements.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the concept asks that only items significant enough to influence the decisions of users be shown separately, so insignificant items may be combined or expensed at once.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm has decided to close down at the end of the month. In the accounts for that month it should still value its machinery on the going concern basis.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The going concern basis assumes the firm will continue. When closure is decided, assets should be valued at the amounts they are expected to realise.

questions.stem_md: At the year end, closing stock is valued at the lower of ___ and ___, following the concept of ___.
questions.solution_md: Closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, which follows the concept of conservatism (prudence): a possible loss is provided for, a possible gain is not recorded.

questions.stem_md: Match each concept in column A with its meaning in column B.

options.text_md: Business entity
Money measurement
Going concern
Accounting period

match_right.text_md: Only events that can be expressed in money are recorded
Profit is worked out for a fixed span, usually a year
The business is treated as separate from its owner
The firm is assumed to continue for the foreseeable future

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Each concept is matched with its standard meaning.

questions.stem_md: Match each convention in column A with the situation in column B that illustrates it.

options.text_md: Full disclosure
Consistency
Conservatism
Materiality

match_right.text_md: A sharpener costing a few rupees is charged to expense at once
A note to the balance sheet reports a pending court claim
A possible loss on stock is provided for but a possible gain is not recorded
The same method of depreciation is followed from year to year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each convention is matched with a situation that shows it at work.

questions.stem_md: Arrange in the correct order the steps in finding the profit of an imagined firm for a month on the matching principle.

options.text_md: Subtract to get the profit or loss of the month
Find the expenses incurred in the month, adjusting payments for outstanding and prepaid amounts
Set the expenses of the month against the revenue of the same month
Find the revenue earned in the month

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). Revenue and expenses of the month are first found on the earned and incurred basis; they are then matched, and the difference is the profit.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Dhruv Cycle Store, an imagined shop, had sales of ₹80,000 in March 2027. Its opening stock was ₹10,000, purchases ₹50,000 and closing stock ₹12,000. Salaries paid in March were ₹7,000, and ₹2,000 of March salary was still to be paid. Rent of ₹15,000 was paid on 1 March for March, April and May. Applying the matching principle, find the profit of March 2027 (in ₹).

Closing stock of an imagined store, Kusum Crockery, has three lots. Lot A: cost ₹15,000, net realisable value ₹18,000. Lot B: cost ₹22,000, net realisable value ₹16,000. Lot C: cost ₹9,000, net realisable value ₹9,000. Valuing lot by lot at the lower of cost and net realisable value, find the value of closing stock (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Lot A = ₹15,000 (cost is lower); Lot B = ₹16,000 (net realisable value is lower); Lot C = ₹9,000. Total = 15,000 + 16,000 + 9,000 = ₹40,000.

questions.stem_md: On 31 March 2027 the assets of Ishani Gift House, an imagined firm, were worth ₹4,20,000. It owed a bank loan of ₹90,000 and ₹45,000 to creditors. Using the accounting equation, find the capital of the proprietor (in ₹).
Define GAAP and state its main purpose.
questions.solution_md: One mark for the meaning, one for the purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: **GAAP**, short for generally accepted accounting principles, means the body of rules, concepts and conventions accepted by accountants for recording transactions and drawing up statements. Its main purpose is uniformity: statements of different firms, and of one firm in different years, become comparable and dependable.

marking_scheme.step: Meaning: accepted rules, concepts and conventions

questions.stem_md: Rekha Sharma runs an imagined tea stall as a sole proprietor. She takes ₹2,500 from the stall's cash box for a family function. Explain how the stall's books should treat this amount under the business entity concept.
questions.solution_md: Separate entity, and the amount treated as drawings.

answer.model_answer_md: Under the business entity concept the stall is a unit separate from Rekha. The ₹2,500 is her personal use of business money, so it is recorded as **drawings**. It reduces the cash of the stall and her capital; it is not an expense of the stall.

marking_scheme.step: Treated as drawings reducing cash and capital, not as an expense

questions.stem_md: State the dual aspect concept. Show its effect on the accounting equation when an imagined firm buys goods worth ₹30,000 on credit.
questions.solution_md: Statement of the concept, then the two equal effects.

answer.model_answer_md: According to the **dual aspect** concept, every transaction has two sides of equal value, so Assets = Liabilities + Capital always holds. On buying goods on credit for ₹30,000, an asset (stock) increases by ₹30,000 and a liability (creditors) increases by ₹30,000.

marking_scheme.step: Two-sided effect of equal value; Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Stock up and creditors up by the same amount

questions.stem_md: Explain the going concern concept and state one effect of it on how an imagined firm records its machinery.
questions.solution_md: The assumption and one effect.

answer.model_answer_md: The **going concern** concept assumes that the firm will continue for the foreseeable future, without intention to close down or shrink greatly. Because of this, machinery is recorded at cost and written off gradually through depreciation over its life, not valued at a forced-sale price.

marking_scheme.step: Machinery at cost less depreciation, not at forced-sale value

questions.stem_md: Ketaki Furnishers, an imagined firm, received an advance of ₹20,000 on 20 November 2026 for a table to be delivered on 5 December 2026, and the balance of ₹15,000 on delivery. State in which month the revenue is recognised, and what the advance is until then.
questions.solution_md: Revenue on delivery; advance is a liability until then.

answer.model_answer_md: Revenue of ₹35,000 is recognised in **December 2026**, when the table is delivered and the sale is complete. Until delivery, the advance of ₹20,000 is not revenue; it is shown as a liability (advance from customer).

marking_scheme.step: Advance is a liability until delivery

questions.stem_md: Harsha Appliances, an imagined shop, has two lots in its closing stock. Toasters: cost ₹18,000, net realisable value ₹21,000. Kettles: cost ₹25,000, net realisable value ₹19,000. Value each lot following conservatism and state the total.
questions.solution_md: Lower of cost and net realisable value for each lot.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Lot | Cost (₹) | Net realisable value (₹) | Valued at (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Toasters | 18,000 | 21,000 | 18,000 |
| Kettles | 25,000 | 19,000 | 19,000 |
| **Total** | **43,000** | **40,000** | **37,000** |

Toasters stay at cost (the gain of ₹3,000 is not recorded); kettles are written down to net realisable value, a loss of ₹6,000 provided for. Closing stock = **₹37,000**.

marking_scheme.step: Kettles at net realisable value and total

questions.stem_md: Explain the concepts of consistency and materiality, giving one imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and example for each concept.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Consistency:** the same accounting methods are followed from year to year so that results can be compared; a change needs a good reason and disclosure. Example: a shop keeps using the straight line method of depreciation every year.

**Materiality:** only items large enough to influence decisions need separate disclosure; trivial items may be treated simply. Example: a pencil sharpener costing ₹40 is charged to expense at once, though it lasts years.

questions.stem_md: Ketan, a partner in Kaveri Printers, an imagined firm, suggests showing its land, bought for ₹18,00,000, in the balance sheet at today's market value of ₹27,00,000. Evaluate the suggestion under the cost concept and give two reasons for recording the land at cost.
questions.solution_md: The rise is not recorded; cost is objective and comparable.

answer.model_answer_md:
The suggestion is **not accepted**. Under the cost concept the land stays at the price paid, ₹18,00,000; the rise of ₹27,00,000 − ₹18,00,000 = ₹9,00,000 (50% of cost) is not recorded because it is not a realised gain.
Reasons for cost:
1. **Objective and verifiable:** the purchase price is supported by a deed and payment record, while a market value is an opinion that changes.
2. **Comparable and free from bias:** different firms report assets on the same basis, and the owner cannot raise profit or capital by choosing a favourable value.

marking_scheme.step: Suggestion rejected, land stays at cost, with the rise worked out

questions.stem_md: Prakash Opticals, an imagined firm, paid rent of ₹60,000 on 1 January 2027 for the twelve months from that date. Its books are closed on 31 March 2027. Find the rent charged to the year, the amount carried forward, and name the concept that decides the charge.
questions.solution_md: Charge for three months, balance prepaid, matching concept.

answer.model_answer_md:
Rent for the year = 60,000 × 3/12 = **₹15,000** (January to March).

Carried forward = 60,000 − 15,000 = **₹45,000**, shown as prepaid rent (an asset) at 31 March 2027.

The concept is **matching**: only the expense that belongs to the period is set against its revenue.

questions.stem_md: The closing stock of Brij Mobiles Mart, an imagined shop, has three lots. Lot P: cost ₹45,000, net realisable value ₹52,000. Lot Q: cost ₹38,000, net realisable value ₹30,000. Lot R: cost ₹27,000, net realisable value ₹27,000. Prepare a statement valuing the stock lot by lot and state the write-down compared with cost.
questions.solution_md: Lower of cost and net realisable value lot by lot.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Lot | Cost (₹) | Net realisable value (₹) | Valued at (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lot P | 45,000 | 52,000 | 45,000 |
| Lot Q | 38,000 | 30,000 | 30,000 |
| Lot R | 27,000 | 27,000 | 27,000 |
| **Total** | **1,10,000** | **1,09,000** | **1,02,000** |

Closing stock = **₹1,02,000**. Write-down compared with cost = 1,10,000 − 1,02,000 = **₹8,000**, from Lot Q only; the unrealised gain on Lot P is not recorded (conservatism).

questions.stem_md: Explain the concepts of business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period and cost, with an imagined illustration of each.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each concept explained with its illustration.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Business entity:** the business is separate from its owner. A shopkeeper's household bill paid from the till is drawings, not an expense.
2. **Money measurement:** only events expressible in money are recorded. A new van bought for ₹4,00,000 is recorded; the skill of the manager is not.
3. **Going concern:** the firm is assumed to continue, so a machine is written off over its life, not valued at a forced-sale price.
4. **Accounting period:** profit and position are found at regular intervals, usually a year, for example 1 April to 31 March.
5. **Cost:** assets are recorded at the price paid; land bought for ₹10,00,000 stays at that figure although its market value rises.

questions.stem_md: Explain the conventions of full disclosure, consistency, conservatism and materiality, and state the effect of each on the accounts of an imagined firm.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and effect of each convention.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Full disclosure:** all information that can influence users must be shown. Effect: a pending claim or a change of method is noted in the statements.
2. **Consistency:** the same methods are used year after year. Effect: results of different years are comparable, and a change needs a reason and disclosure.
3. **Conservatism:** anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses. Effect: closing stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
4. **Materiality:** only significant items need separate treatment. Effect: a trivial purchase is charged to expense at once, while a major asset is capitalised.
Together they make the statements reliable and useful without overloading them.

questions.stem_md: Ridhi Gift Corner, an imagined shop, starts business with cash of ₹2,00,000 as the proprietor's capital. It then (i) buys fixtures for ₹60,000 cash, (ii) buys goods for ₹45,000 on credit, (iii) sells goods that cost ₹20,000 for ₹26,000 cash, and (iv) pays ₹25,000 to creditors. Show the effect of each transaction on the accounting equation and verify that it holds at the end.
questions.solution_md: Each transaction changes two items by equal amounts; the profit on the sale goes to capital.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Transaction | Cash (₹) | Fixtures (₹) | Stock (₹) | Creditors (₹) | Capital (₹) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bought fixtures for cash ₹60,000 | 1,40,000 | 60,000 | 0 | 0 | 2,00,000 |
| Bought goods on credit ₹45,000 | 1,40,000 | 60,000 | 45,000 | 45,000 | 2,00,000 |
| Sold goods costing ₹20,000 for cash ₹26,000 | 1,66,000 | 60,000 | 25,000 | 45,000 | 2,06,000 |
| Paid creditors ₹25,000 | 1,41,000 | 60,000 | 25,000 | 20,000 | 2,06,000 |

Total assets = 1,41,000 + 60,000 + 25,000 = ₹2,26,000. Liabilities (creditors) + Capital = 20,000 + 2,06,000 = ₹2,26,000. The equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital holds. In (iii) capital rises by the profit of ₹6,000.

marking_scheme.step: Transaction (iii) with profit added to capital
Closing totals of assets, liabilities and capital

questions.stem_md: Bhoomi Bakers, an imagined bakery, had sales of ₹95,000 in March 2027, part of it on credit. Opening stock was ₹8,000, purchases ₹41,000 and closing stock ₹9,000. Wages paid were ₹14,000, with ₹2,000 of March wages unpaid. On 1 March it paid rent of ₹18,000 for March, April and May. Electricity of ₹2,000 was paid for March. Applying the matching principle, find the profit of March 2027 and the rent carried forward.
questions.solution_md: Revenue earned less expenses incurred for the month.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Revenue: sales of the month | 95,000 |
| Less: cost of goods sold (8,000 + 41,000 − 9,000) | 40,000 |
| Less: wages (14,000 paid + 2,000 due) | 16,000 |
| Less: rent of March (18,000 ÷ 3) | 6,000 |
| Less: electricity | 2,000 |
| **Profit of March 2027** | **31,000** |

Rent carried forward as a prepaid expense = 18,000 − 6,000 = **₹12,000**. Credit sales are included in revenue because the sale is made, even though cash is yet to come.

marking_scheme.step: Rent of one month and electricity; profit

questions.stem_md: Under the cash basis of accounting, rent of ₹10,000 for March 2027 that an imagined firm pays on 5 April 2027 is recorded as an expense of

options.text_md: March 2027, the month to which the rent relates
April 2027, the month in which cash is paid
March and April equally
neither month, since no benefit arises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** April 2027, the month in which cash is paid. On the cash basis an item is recorded when cash moves. Relating it to March is the accrual basis; splitting it has no basis in either method, and rent plainly gives a benefit.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes the accrual basis of accounting?

options.text_md: Revenue and expenses are recorded only when cash is received or paid
Revenue is recorded when earned, but expenses only when paid
Expenses are recorded when incurred, but revenue only when cash is received
Revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash moves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, whether or not cash moves. Accrual accounting follows the earning of revenue and the incurring of expenses. The second option describes the cash basis and the last two mix the bases.

questions.stem_md: Ravi Foods and Sneha Foods, two imagined companies, value their stock by different methods without saying so, and their profits cannot be compared. Which purpose of accounting standards would remove this difficulty?

options.text_md: Reducing alternative treatments, so that accounts are comparable
Guaranteeing a profit to every company
Replacing the need for an audit
Fixing the selling price of goods

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Reducing alternative treatments, so that accounts are comparable. Standards narrow the choice of methods and ask for disclosure of the method used, so statements become comparable. They cannot guarantee profit, replace an audit, or fix prices.

questions.stem_md: In India, accounting standards are issued by the

options.text_md: Reserve Bank of India, through its monetary policy committee
Goods and Services Tax Council, through its tax boards
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, through its Accounting Standards Board
Central Board of Direct Taxes, through its audit wing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, through its Accounting Standards Board. The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) issues accounting standards through its Accounting Standards Board. The other bodies deal with money and credit, indirect tax rates and income tax.

questions.stem_md: Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) are described as being converged with

options.text_md: the accounting rules of one single foreign country
the rules of the Income Tax Act
International Financial Reporting Standards
the cost accounting records of each firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** International Financial Reporting Standards. Ind AS are Indian standards brought into line with International Financial Reporting Standards. They are not copied from one country, nor are they tax rules or cost records.

questions.stem_md: Goods and services tax is called a destination-based tax. This means that the tax

options.text_md: accrues to the state where the goods or services are finally consumed
is collected only at the place where the goods are manufactured
is paid only by importers at the port of entry
is charged only on goods sent out of the country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** accrues to the state where the goods or services are finally consumed. In a destination-based tax the revenue goes to the place of consumption. The other options describe origin-based collection, import duty and export, none of which is the meaning.

questions.stem_md: Dev Hardware, an imagined firm in Jaipur (Rajasthan), sells goods to a trader in Surat (Gujarat). The goods and services tax charged on this supply is

options.text_md: central and state goods and services tax (CGST and SGST), half each
state goods and services tax (SGST) only
central goods and services tax (CGST) only
integrated goods and services tax (IGST)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** integrated goods and services tax (IGST). A supply from one state to another is an inter-state supply and attracts IGST. CGST and SGST together apply to supplies within one state, and neither alone is charged on an inter-state supply.

questions.stem_md: In a month, an imagined trader paid ₹9,000 as goods and services tax on purchases and collected ₹14,000 on sales. Using input tax credit, the tax payable to the government is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹5,000. Input tax credit sets the tax paid on purchases against the tax collected on sales: 14,000 − 9,000 = ₹5,000. ₹14,000 ignores the credit, ₹9,000 is the credit itself, and ₹23,000 adds the two.

questions.stem_md: The goods and services tax identification number (GSTIN) of a registered taxpayer has

options.text_md: 15 characters, including the state code and the PAN of the taxpayer
10 digits, being the mobile number of the owner
the same number for every taxpayer in a state
5 characters chosen freely by the taxpayer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 15 characters, including the state code and the PAN of the taxpayer. As of 2024 a GSTIN has 15 characters, beginning with a two-digit state code followed by the taxpayer's PAN. It is unique to the registration, not a mobile number, not shared, and not self-chosen.

questions.stem_md: Goods and services tax was introduced in India with effect from

options.text_md: 1 April 2010
1 July 2017
1 January 2020

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meaning:** accounting standards are written statements of uniform accounting rules and policies for the treatment and disclosure of items in financial statements.
